summary.text: Zeus, falling in love with the Phoenician princess Europa, took the form of a tame white bull and bore her across the sea to Crete, where she bore Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon — and her father Agenor sent Cadmus and his brothers to wander the world until they found her, seeding the Cadmean search for Thebes.

chapters.title: Agenor's daughter
chapters.text: Agenor went to Phoenicia, married Telephassa, and begat a daughter Europa and three sons, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix. But some say Europa was a daughter not of Agenor but of Phoenix — and Homer makes her daughter of Phoenix and niece of Cadmus, not sister. The genealogies divide; the abduction is the same in every telling.

chapters.title: The tame bull
chapters.text: Zeus loved her. Ovid tells how the god, fearing jealous Juno, changed himself to a bull — snow-white, gentle-eyed, horns gilded, no trace of fear upon his brow — and mingled with the herds on the grass. Europa and her maidens wove garlands for the creature; when she climbed onto its back the bull plunged into the sea and swam away from the shore. Apollodorus says simply that Zeus turned himself into a tame bull, mounted her on his back, and conveyed her through the sea to Crete.

chapters.title: Crete and the Cretan kings
chapters.text: In Crete Zeus lay with Europa, and she bore Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthus — though Homer makes Sarpedon son of Zeus by Laodamia daughter of Bellerophon, not by Europa. Asterius prince of the Cretans married her and brought up her children; when they were grown they quarrelled over a boy called Miletus. Agenor meanwhile sent Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix to search for Europa and forbade their return without her — the quest that would end not in Phoenicia but at Apollo's cow in Boeotia.
